citations.cited_for: Inadvertent disclosure does not waive privilege
citations.context: shall not constitute a waiver of the privilege or protection as to the disclosed information or any related information, in accordance with Fed. R. Evid. 502(b).

first_check.explanation: Fed. R. Evid. 502(b) is the inadvertent-disclosure provision and supports the proposition that an inadvertent disclosure does not operate as a waiver. Caveat: the model objection states non-waiver categorically ('any inadvertent disclosure ... shall not constitute a waiver'), while 502(b) makes non-waiver conditional on three elements (inadvertence, reasonable steps to prevent, prompt reasonable steps to rectify). A unilateral reservation does not change those requirements. Also, the 'or any related information' clause concerns subject-matter waiver, which is governed by 502(a), not 502(b). Read as standard reservation boilerplate invoking the rule ('in accordance with'), the citation is fair; a stricter reader could call it a minor defect for omitting the conditions. The same document states the three conditions accurately elsewhere (section VIII.C).

Rockwell Int'l, 897 F.2d 1255, at *1266 (page marker confirmed in the CourtListener text). Also found verbatim, citing Rockwell at 1266, in Montgomery County v. MicroVote Corp., 175 F.3d 296 (3d Cir. 1999) (concurrence) and Sharp v. Gov't of the Virgin Islands, 77 F. App'x 82 (3d Cir. 2003).
first_check.explanation: No citation accompanies this sentence in the memo, so I checked the doctrine itself. The associate's statement that the claim 'may fail' under this test is a fair application. The Third Circuit's analogous standard ... asks whether "in light of the nature of the document and the factual situation in the particular case, the document can fairly be said to have been prepared or obtained because of the prospect of litigation."

citations.cited_for: Privilege log required for information withheld under attorney-client privilege or the work product doctrine
citations.context: If You claim that any responsive information is protected by the attorney-client privilege, the work product doctrine, or any other applicable privilege or protection, You must provide a privilege log

first_check.explanation: This is a doctrinal reference rather than a reporter citation; the instruction itself anchors it to Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(b)(5)(A), which I read. That rule requires a party withholding otherwise discoverable information as privileged or as trial-preparation (work product) material to expressly make the claim and describe the withheld items in a manner that lets other parties assess the claim. That is the privilege-log obligation as commonly understood, and the instruction's 'sufficient detail to allow Tri-Basin to assess the claim of privilege' tracks the rule's language. Work product protection is itself codified at Rule 26(b)(3)(A). One nuance that does not undermine support: the rule does not use the term 'privilege log' or mandate the six specific fields the instruction lists 'at a minimum'; the 1993 committee note says the rule does not define what information must be provided and that such details 'may be appropriate' for a small number of items but may be unduly burdensome for voluminous withholdings. The field list is the propounding party's own demand, not something attributed to the rule.
first_check.evidence_excerpt: Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(b)(5)(A): "When a party withholds information otherwise discoverable by claiming that the information is privileged or subject to protection as trial-preparation material, the party must: (i) expressly make the claim; and (ii) describe the nature of the documents, communications, or tangible things not produced or disclosed—and do so in a manner that, without revealing information itself privileged or protected, will enable other parties to assess the claim."

citations.context: All *Daubert* motions shall comply with the applicable page limits set forth in the Local Rules of this Court.

first_check.correct_citation: Page limits for briefs in W.D. Pa. are set by the assigned judge's Practices and Procedures (which LCvR 7.A requires motions to comply with) or by order, e.g., Judge Ranjan's Practices and Procedures (rev. 3/10/23) § II.i (principal brief no more than 20 pages); the W.D. Pa. Local Civil Rules themselves set no page limits for Daubert motions.
first_check.explanation: The Local Rules of Court for the W.D. Pa. exist, but the full text (130-page manual, eff. Nov. 1, 2016, the version linked as current on the court's local-rules page) contains no page limits for motions or briefs. A full-text search for 'page', 'pages', 'length', 'words', and 'limit' returned no brief-length provision in LCvR 7 (motion practice), LCvR 16.1.C.4 (motions in limine), or anywhere else. LCvR 7.A instead sends parties to the assigned judge's posted practices and procedures, which is where page limits live (the court's own brief-writing guide tells counsel to 'Determine whether the Judge has established page limitations'; Judge Ranjan's procedures set a 20-page limit). So the CMO's reference to page limits 'set forth in the Local Rules of this Court' points to a rule the authority does not contain. Mitigating point: the word 'applicable' makes the sentence conditional, and LCvR 7.A does indirectly incorporate chambers page limits, so a generous reader could treat this as loose drafting rather than a wrong citation; I did not adopt that reading because the limits are not 'set forth in' the Local Rules. Caveat: I relied on the version of the rules currently posted by the court; I did not locate any later amendment adding page limits.
first_check.evidence_excerpt: LCvR 7.A: "Motions in all civil actions pending in this Court shall comply with the applicable Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, the applicable Local Rules, the orders of the assigned Judge and the practices and procedures of the assigned Judge that are posted at the following internet link" | Judge Ranjan P&P § II.i: "Unless ordered otherwise, the principal brief in support of a motion should be no more than 20 pages."

second_check.explanation: I could not refute this finding. I downloaded the court's posted Local Rules of Court (130 pages, 'Effective: November 1, 2016'). The court's local-rules page lists this as the current version; the only later item is a set of proposed amendments published 9/11/2026, which postdates this 2024-25 CMO and is not yet in force. I searched the full text for 'page', 'word', 'length' and 'limit' and found no length limit for motions or briefs anywhere. The 'page' hits concern formatting (LCvR 5.1: page numbers, page fasteners) or record citations. LCvR 7 (Motion Practice) sets no limit; it says only that motions 'shall comply with the applicable Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, the applicable Local Rules, the orders of the assigned Judge and the practices and procedures of the assigned Judge that are posted at' the chambers webpage. Page limits therefore come from judges' posted procedures, not the Local Rules. The CMO says Daubert motions 'shall comply with the applicable page limits set forth in the Local Rules of this Court', which credits the Local Rules with a provision they do not contain. The word 'applicable', and the fact that LCvR 7.A indirectly brings in chambers procedures, make this loose drafting rather than an invented rule. That is mitigation, not refutation: the limits are not 'set forth in' the Local Rules.

citations.context: Dispositive motions, including motions for summary judgment under Fed. R. Civ. P. 56, shall be filed no later than March 1, 2025.

first_check.explanation: Rule 56 is the summary judgment rule, so the order's reference to "motions for summary judgment under Fed. R. Civ. P. 56" is accurate. Rule 56(b) also expressly allows the court to set the filing time by order, which is consistent with the order fixing a dispositive-motion deadline.

citations.citation_as_written: Local Rules of the United States District Court for the Western District of Pennsylvania
citations.cited_for: Dispositive motions comply with page limits
citations.context: must comply with the page limits set forth in the Local Rules of the United States District Court for the Western District of Pennsylvania.

first_check.correct_citation: Page limits for dispositive-motion briefs in W.D. Pa. are set by the assigned judge's Practices and Procedures (which LCvR 7.A requires motions to comply with) or by order, e.g., Judge Ranjan's Practices and Procedures (rev. 3/10/23) § II.i (principal brief no more than 20 pages); LCvR 56 governs summary judgment content and timing but sets no page limits. (Separately, the CMO's adjacent 'Local Rule 56.1' is styled LCvR 56 in this district.)
first_check.explanation: The Local Rules of the U.S. District Court for the W.D. Pa. exist, but they set no page limits for dispositive motions or supporting briefs. I read LCvR 56 in full: it requires a motion, a separately filed concise statement of material facts, a supporting memorandum, and an appendix, with a 30-day opposition and 14-day reply, and says nothing about length. LCvR 7 likewise has no page limit; LCvR 7.A directs compliance with the assigned judge's posted practices and procedures. A full-text search of the 130-page rules manual for 'page', 'pages', 'length', 'words', and 'limit' found no brief-length provision. The CMO's unqualified statement that briefs 'must comply with the page limits set forth in the Local Rules' therefore attributes to the rules a provision they do not contain; the operative limits come from chambers procedures (Judge Ranjan: 20 pages for a principal brief) or briefing orders. Mitigating point: LCvR 7.A indirectly incorporates chambers limits, so this could be read as loose drafting, but unlike ref 131 this sentence has no 'applicable' qualifier. Caveat: I relied on the version of the rules currently posted by the court (eff. Nov. 1, 2016) and found no later amendment adding page limits.
first_check.evidence_excerpt: LCvR 56.B.2: "Memorandum in Support. The supporting memorandum must address applicable law and explain why there are no genuine issues of material fact to be tried and why the moving party is entitled to judgment as a matter of law" (no length provision) | Court brief-writing guide checklist: "Determine whether the Judge has established page limitations regarding the brief and, if so, be prepared to comply with them or seek leave to exceed the page limit for good cause."

second_check.explanation: I could not refute this finding. In the posted W.D. Pa. Local Rules (effective Nov. 1, 2016; the only later item is a set of proposed amendments published 9/11/2026), I read LCvR 56 in full. It requires a motion that sets out 'succinctly, but without argument, the specific grounds', a separately filed Concise Statement of Material Facts in 'separately numbered paragraphs', a supporting memorandum and an appendix. The opposition is due 'Within 30 days' and the reply 'Within 14 days'. It sets no page limit. LCvR 7 also sets no limit; LCvR 7.A defers to 'the orders of the assigned Judge and the practices and procedures of the assigned Judge'. A full-text search for 'page', 'word', 'length' and 'limit' found no provision on brief length. The CMO flatly says dispositive motions and briefs 'must comply with the page limits set forth in the Local Rules of the United States District Court for the Western District of Pennsylvania', which credits the rules with content they lack. This is a real authority cited for a rule it does not contain, so MISCHARACTERIZED stands. A side point the first reviewer also noted: the CMO's adjacent 'Local Rule 56.1' is styled LCvR 56 (subsections 56.B.1 and 56.C.1 cover concise statements).

citations.cited_for: Concise statements of material facts and responses
citations.context: Concise statements of material facts and responses thereto must be filed in accordance with Local Rule 56.1.

first_check.correct_citation: LCvR 56.B.1 and 56.C.1 (W.D. Pa.) (the rule is numbered LCvR 56; there is no LCvR 56.1)
first_check.explanation: The substance is accurate but the rule number is wrong. The Western District of Pennsylvania has no rule numbered 56.1: a search of the full Local Rules manual returns zero hits for '56.1', and the only summary judgment rule is 'LCvR 56 Motion for Summary Judgment.' That rule does exactly what the CMO describes: 56.B.1 requires a separately filed Concise Statement of Material Facts in separately numbered paragraphs with record citations, and 56.C.1 requires a Responsive Concise Statement answering each numbered paragraph with record references. The CMO's own description (separately numbered paragraphs, specific record citations, paragraph-by-paragraph response) tracks LCvR 56.B.1 and 56.C.1 closely. '56.1' is the numbering other districts use. Checked against the manual the court's website currently posts (effective Nov. 1, 2016).
first_check.evidence_excerpt: "LCvR 56 MOTION FOR SUMMARY JUDGMENT ... B. ... 1. A Concise Statement of Material Facts. A separately filed concise statement setting forth the facts essential for the Court to decide the motion ... shall be stated in separately numbered paragraphs." "C. ... 1. A Responsive Concise Statement. A separately filed concise statement, which responds to each numbered paragraph in the moving party's Concise Statement of Material Facts"

citations.cited_for: Joint pretrial statement conforms to Local Rule 16.1
citations.context: The joint pretrial statement shall conform to the requirements of Local Rule 16.1

first_check.explanation: W.D. Pa. LCvR 16.1 ('Pretrial Procedures') exists, and subpart 16.1.C ('Pretrial Statements and Final Pretrial Conference') prescribes what a pretrial statement must contain (narrative of material facts, damages, witness lists, deposition designations, exhibits, legal issues, expert disclosures). A CMO directing that the pretrial statement conform to Local Rule 16.1 is accurate. Small mismatch that does not undermine the cite: the rule contemplates sequential separate statements (plaintiff first, defendant within 30 days), not a 'joint' statement, and the court's formal designation is 'LCvR 16.1'; the operative subpart is 16.1.C. Checked against the Local Rules manual the court's website currently posts (effective Nov. 1, 2016).
first_check.evidence_excerpt: "C. Pretrial Statements and Final Pretrial Conference. 1. By the date specified in the Court's scheduling order ... counsel for the plaintiff or an unrepresented plaintiff shall file and serve a pretrial statement. The pretrial statement shall include: a. a brief narrative statement of the material facts that will be offered at trial"

citations.cited_for: Sanctions for noncompliance with the Order
citations.context: Failure to comply with this Order may result in sanctions, including those authorized under Fed. R. Civ. P. 16(f) and 37

first_check.quote_check: No quotations attributed to this citation.
first_check.explanation: Rule 16(f)(1)(C) authorizes "any just orders," including those in Rule 37(b)(2)(A)(ii)-(vii), when a party or its attorney fails to obey a scheduling or other pretrial order, and 16(f)(2) requires an award of reasonable expenses including attorney's fees. Rule 37(b)(2)(A) lists preclusion of evidence, striking pleadings, and dismissal. The sanctions the Case Management Order names (dismissal of claims, striking of defenses, preclusion of evidence, fees and costs) all appear in those provisions, so the citation supports the proposition.
first_check.evidence_excerpt: On motion or on its own, the court may issue any just orders, including those authorized by Rule 37(b)(2)(A)(ii)-(vii), if a party or its attorney: ... (C) fails to obey a scheduling or other pretrial order.
